Our agent found a bug that could've stolen $60 million at the time. Claude and Codex both missed it. In Aleo ’s snarkVM, a missing Fiat-Shamir absorb enabled arbitrary proof forgery meaning an attacker could send any transaction from any public wallet address. Our agent traced it from a 500,000+ line codebase to a full end to end PoC in a single run that showed the ability to steal all the money from a wallet it doesn't own. We responsibly disclosed it, Aleo patched it immediately and were able to confirm all funds are safe and this vulnerability was never exploited in production. Maximum bug bounty awarded from Immunefi : $65,000 ...more ...more

Spent the afternoon in SF with Anna Y. Zhang and a group of YC founders talking about self-improving software. I shared The Boring Orchestrator, a small internal tool we open-sourced at Nessie Labs . The idea is simple: keep the orchestrator tiny. It wakes agents up, runs lightweight pre-scripts to check whether there's actually work to do before spending tokens, records what happened, and pushes the real work into Claude Code or Codex. The part I'm most convinced by: don't build a new harness or message bus unless you absolutely have to. Use the coding agents, skills, subscriptions, tools, and systems your team already lives in. PRs welcome: https://lnkd.in/gxaCTDTX Big thanks to Milan Stankovic and Erik Dahl for hosting. ...more ...more

Would you trust a chef who wouldn't eat their own food? I wouldn't either. So why should I expect anyone to use MyTrials.ai if I haven't used it myself? That's why, when Tyler built a new feature to enrol healthy volunteers, Omar and I tested it ourselves as real participants, not as a demo or a test account. It's easy to build a product, put together a pitch, and go promote it. It's much harder to sit in your users' seat and feel every point of friction yourself. Going through our platform as a participant gave me the ability to advocate for it honestly. So when I tell a patient advocacy group that we make trial participation easier, I'm not repeating a talking point, I'm speaking from experience. If you're looking to contribute to new treatments, we're working on a feature that lets you enrol in trials looking for healthy volunteers. Omar and I took 20 minutes of our lunch break to give blood. You (and your coworkers :)) can too. #ClinicalTrials #DrugDevelopment #StartUpLife

Customers were ignoring half of our product. Some of our happiest customers who loved Replicas used it as a pure background agent. Firing off long tasks from Slack or API, close the tab, and come back later. Replicas did ~40% of their pull requests - which was amazing, but I wanted to know how we could do the other 60%. So I went to every customer office I could get into and asked why. They answered with one word: Latency It wasn't quality. Cloud agents were finishing the same tasks as well or better than a local run. But a terminal 'started' faster, and when someone wants a two-minute fix they reach for whatever starts faster. Ultimately, the company that wins cloud will be the one with the best UX. Last week, we reworked the flow with principled caching and incorporated optimistic UI. Now, every user can create and send messages literally nearly instantaneously - with less than 2 seconds of waiting between the first token and the message being sent. As founders, we'd love to just hack our way into users' hearts. Make more features, fix bugs, and prettier UI. But sometimes, customers will use you just because it 'feels' better - whatever that ends up meaning.

Tom Blomfield was our YC partner. He just joined Anthropic . Before YC he built GoCardless , then Monzo . He could have done anything after that. What he did was sit in a room with stressed out founders every two weeks and ask what was in their way. The first thing he told us was to stop bringing him updates. He wanted problems and bottlenecks. So we brought him one. Manu Ebert and I had been circling the same decision for weeks. We had a business that was working and a much bigger opportunity we were excited about, and we'd built a whole case for why we couldn't commit to the second without abandoning the first. Tom listened to all of it, then asked what it would actually cost us, in people, to keep the first business running well while we went after the second. That was the question we had been avoiding. We answered it in about thirty seconds and the rest of the decision fell out of it. That was the pattern with Tom. We'd come in with five competing worries and leave with one concrete thing to do. When we were spiraling over something, he'd tell us he'd seen this movie before, and ask a few questions that brought us to clarity. By the time we finished talking, the right move felt obvious. That conversation is the reason Hyperspell is building the company brain for enterprises today. Tom also never stopped being a builder. He knew our customers by name, which I still don't understand given how many companies he was supporting, and he'd reply within the hour on a Saturday. During our raise he went line by line with me on individual investor emails. He went to YC after Monzo instead of becoming a full time investor, and now he's going to Anthropic to build again. Congrats, Tom.
